question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question names a specific format (best of five games to 11), so the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11, govern first. Its clause 8.1.3 states the change of ends for the third game in that format: at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game — there is no mid-game switch at 11 in this format. The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clause 8.1.3 (third game when a side first scores 11) is explicitly the clause this alternative replaces ('alternative to: laws-8.1.3'), so it does not apply here. Both parts of the question (when in the third game, in this format) are answered by alt-best-of-5-games-11:8.1.3.
answer.answer: In a best-of-five-games-to-11 match, in the third game you switch ends at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game (Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, in force 2027-01-04, format best-of-5-games-11, Law 8.1.3). The general Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 8.1.3, which require changing ends in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, do not apply to this format, because the best-of-5-games-11 clause is the alternative to that law.

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens when the opponent shouts 'fault!' while you are playing your shot. laws-13.4.5 makes deliberate distraction of an opponent in play, such as shouting, a fault. itto-5.9.1.4 specifies that a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5 — exactly this scenario, since the opponent shouted at you during your stroke. laws-7.3 gives the consequence: a side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, and the side winning a rally adds a point to its score. So the ruling is a fault against your opponent and a point to you. The itto-5.9.1.3 exception (shouting to a partner) does not apply because the shout was directed at the opponent.
answer.answer: Your opponent's shout of 'fault!' while you were playing your shot is a deliberate distraction, which is a fault against your opponent: under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 13.4.5, "if, in play, a player: deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures". The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.4, confirm that "A player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)". Because your opponent committed a fault, you win the rally and score a point: under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 7.3, "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’" and "The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score".

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) when a rally is replayed — answered by Law 14.3 (play since the last service shall not count and the last server serves again) and Law 14.1 (who calls a let); (2) every situation that counts as a let — answered by the complete list in Law 14.2, sub-clauses 14.2.1 through 14.2.7, including the two net situations under 14.2.3 (14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2). Law 14.2.1 cross-refers to Law 9.4 for the receiver-ready condition, so laws-9.4 was read to state that requirement fully. All parts have sources; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: A 'let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Law 14.1, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26). When a 'let' occurs, the rally is replayed: play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again (Law 14.3). It shall be a 'let' (Law 14.2) in each of these situations: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready — and the receiver is considered ready if a return of the service is attempted (Law 9.4); (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top; (4) after the service is returned, the shuttle, after passing over the net, is caught in the net; (5) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle; (6) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach; (7) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or (8) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play may stop for a bleeding injury — answered by laws-16.3.1 (umpire's suspension power), itto-5.14.2 (blood-flowing injury delay), itto-3.6.1.4 (resolve well within a few minutes), itto-5.14.1 (umpire times the delay; no undue-delay treatment), itto-3.6.1.2 (quick relief only, no time-consuming treatment outside intervals), and itto-3.6.1.6 (severe-injury exception); (2) who may come on court — answered by itto-5.14.1 (Referee decides who is required), itto-3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court when called), and itto-3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons to assist, same consideration for the opposing side). All parts have sources, so refused is false.
answer.answer:
How long you can stop: Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1, "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary." For your partner's bleeding hand specifically, the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2 state: "For a blood flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise." There is no fixed number of minutes: Clause 3.6.1.4 says "The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned," and Clause 5.14.1 says "The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury." On treatment, Clause 3.6.1.2 says: "The Tournament Doctor may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals and then only if the Tournament Doctor estimates that the treatment can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends." If the injury is severe and there is no doubt your partner cannot continue, Clause 3.6.1.6 says: "In case of a severe injury, where there is no doubt that the player cannot continue, the regular process (Instructions 3.6.1.2 - 3.6.1.4) shall be disregarded, and the Tournament Doctor shall provide the necessary first aid until the player can be transported to hospital."

Who can come on court to help: Clause 5.14.1 says "The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6)," after the Umpire calls the Referee onto court. Clause 3.6.1.1 says: "When called by the Umpire in case of injury or illness, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court." Beyond them, Clause 3.6.1.3 says: "The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation," and adds that "In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration" — so your opponents are entitled to the same help if they need it.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: what happens to the match (play) and what happens to the score when water drips onto the court mid-game. Sources found: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Clause 14.2.7 makes any unforeseen or accidental situation a 'let', and Clause 14.3 says play since the last service does not count and the last server serves again. Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) Clause 5.11.2 allows suspension by Referee or Umpire when a circumstance affects playing conditions; Clause 5.11.3 requires the Umpire to call the Referee and suspend play until the court is again suitable if it is temporarily not playable; Clause 5.11.4 gives the 'Play is suspended' call; Clause 5.11.5 gives the resumption procedure; Clause 5.10.4 covers wiping/mopping the court. Laws of Badminton Clause 16.3.3 states that if play is suspended the existing score stands and play resumes from that point. Together these answer both parts: the rally in progress is a let (no score, replayed) and/or play is suspended until the court is wiped and suitable, with the score standing in either case.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court mid-game is an unforeseen or accidental situation, so it shall be a 'let' (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 14.2.7: "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred."). When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 14.3: "When a ‘let’ occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again."), so no point is awarded to you or your opponent for that rally and the score is unchanged. If the court or its immediate surroundings is temporarily not playable, play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.2: "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions."), and the Umpire shall call the Referee and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.3: "If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play."). When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call "Play is suspended" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.4: "When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended”..."), and the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 16.3.3: "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point."). If the court needs to be wiped, you and your opponent shall indicate to the Court Attendants where mopping is needed and be on court as soon as the wiping is over (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.10.4: "If the court needs to be wiped, the players shall indicate to the Court Attendants where mopping is needed. The players shall be on court as soon as the wiping is over and before the Court Attendants leave the court."). When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension, ensure you and your opponent are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.11.5: "When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”."). In short: the rally in progress is replayed as a let with no point to either side, play may be suspended until the wet court is wiped and suitable again, and in every case the score you and your opponent had stands unchanged.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when the opponent repeatedly flicks sweat onto the court. The directly on-point source is ITTO clause 5.9.1.6, which names 'a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court' and says the umpire shall remind the player and apply Law 16.7 if necessary. Law 16.7.1 and its sub-clauses (Laws of Badminton 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3) give the escalation ladder the umpire administers for a breach of Law 16.6: warning, fault if previously warned, fault for flagrant offence. Law 16.7.2 adds that on faulting, the umpire reports to the Referee, who may disqualify the offending side. ITTO 5.17.3 and 5.17.4 give the on-court procedure (yellow card for warning, red card plus calling the Referee for a fault). answer.answer: The umpire must first remind your opponent that the conduct is unacceptable: under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.6, "A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary". If it continues, the umpire administers the breach under Law 16.7 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: the umpire shall administer any breach of Law 16.6 by "issuing a warning to the offending side" (Law 16.7.1.1), by "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" (Law 16.7.1.2), or by "faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach" (Law 16.7.1.3). Because your opponent keeps doing it, once a warning has been issued the next breach is a fault against your opponent's side. The warning is delivered by calling "Come here" to the offending player and calling "… [name of player], warning for misconduct" while raising a yellow card (ITTO 5.17.3); a fault is called as "… [name of player], fault for misconduct" with a red card, and the umpire must call the Referee on court and report immediately (ITTO 5.17.4). On faulting your opponent's side, "the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match" (Law 16.7.2). The underlying prohibition is Law 16.6: "A player shall not: behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner" (Law 16.6.3) or "be guilty of misconduct not otherwise covered by the Laws of Badminton" (Law 16.6.4).

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when the line judge could not see the shuttle's landing. laws-14.2.6 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.2) states it is a 'let' if a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision. itto-2.5 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) adds that when another official is unsighted the Umpire shall make the decision, and when no decision can be made a 'let' shall be called unless IRS is in use. laws-14.3 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 14.3) states what a let means for the rally: play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again. Together these answer the question fully; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: If the line judge is unsighted, the Umpire makes the decision; if the Umpire (or the Instant Review System, when in use) is unable to make a decision, it is a 'let' — "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.2.6), and "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision. When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 2.5). When a 'let' occurs, the rally does not count: "play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again" (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.3). So for you and your opponent, no point is scored either way and the same server serves the rally again.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. ITTO 7.0 (5) clause 5.12.2 (in force 2025-04-26), under '5.12 Coaching from Off Court', directly answers this: coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2). Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clauses 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 define those permitted intervals (60 seconds at 11 points in a game; 120 seconds between games). All parts of the question are covered; no part is missing.
answer.answer: No. Your coach must stay seated in his designated seat and must not stand at the side of the court during the match, except during the permitted intervals: the interval of not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, and the interval of not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game and between the second and third game. (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2; Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clauses 16.2.1 and 16.2.2.)

answer.answer: Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, a plastic/synthetic shuttle is a non-feathered shuttle: its skirt is a simulation of feathers in synthetic materials. question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) Whether a yellow card for misconduct during the warm-up, before 'Play', costs a point: itto-5.17.10 directly covers misconduct before the match on the Field of Play before 'Play' and states any card has no effect on the score but is taken into account for further offences during the match; laws-16.7.1.1 and laws-16.7.1.2 confirm a warning is the first step and faulting (which costs a point) applies only if previously warned; itto-5.17.3 confirms the yellow card is the warning. The warm-up timing is confirmed by itto-5.2.2.1 (warm-up ends with the calling of 'Play') and itto-5.3.2 ('Play' indicates the start of the match). (2) Whether the card goes on the record after the tournament: itto-3.7.3 requires the Referee to report yellow and red cards to BWF (or CC) immediately after the tournament, which may trigger further sanctions, with the exception in itto-3.7.3.1 allowing the Referee not to report a card in a specific observed case. Both parts are answered; refused is false.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost your opponent a point now. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" has been called is administered as a warning, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)" [itto-5.17.10]. The Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, confirm the sequence: the umpire administers a breach "issuing a warning to the offending side; or" and only "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" [laws-16.7.1.1, laws-16.7.1.2], and the yellow card is raised when issuing that warning [itto-5.17.3]. So the card only matters against your opponent if he commits further offences during the match, in which case his side is faulted. (The warm-up period is the two minutes ending with the calling of "Play" [itto-5.2.2.1], and the calling of "Play" indicates the start of the match [itto-5.3.2], so your scenario is exactly the pre-"Play" case.) As for the record after the tournament: yes, the card is reported. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions" [itto-3.7.3], so your opponent's yellow card goes into that report and may trigger further sanctions; the only exception is that "The Referee may decide not to report a card given by an Umpire, if the Referee or a Deputy has observed the situation where the card was given and decides that the card should not have been issued" [itto-3.7.3.1].
